description: The project monitors astronauts' health indicators based on selected risks. It establishes a personalized health baseline then detects deviations and uses NASA HRP-informed thresholds. The system identify unusual patterns across multiple indicators, even when self-reported alertness differs from actual performance. provides explainable alerts with evidence-based recommendations.
summary:
crew health monitoring system that turns daily astronaut data into alerts the right person can act on, with NASA evidence behind every threshold.

We built a knowledge base from six NASA Human Research Program Evidence Reports and NASA-STD-3001: 49 health indicators across 21 HRP risks, and 76 values, each traced to its document, page and exact quote.

The engine reads crew measurements (sleep, reaction time, mood, heart rate, radiation dose) alongside real NASA data: DONKI space weather, RadLab ISS radiation and OSDR cabin telemetry. It compares each astronaut against NASA thresholds and their own baseline, flags unusual combinations, and routes each alert by severity: yellow to the astronaut, orange to the crew medical officer, red to the flight surgeon. Every alert shows its reason, a recommended action and its source.
details:
What it does and how it works
ORVITALIS is health monitoring software for astronauts. Every day, it turns crew and mission data into one alert level per astronaut and sends it to the person who must act. Yellow goes to the astronaut, orange to the crew medical officer, and red to the flight surgeon.

It works in five steps:

  1. Knowledge base. We read six NASA HRP Evidence Reports and NASA-STD-3001 Volumes 1 and 2. From them we extracted 76 values, each with its document, page and exact quote.
  2. Inputs. API endpoints receive crew readings (sleep, reaction time, mood, heart rate), cabin and radiation telemetry, and space weather.
  3. Engine. It computes daily features such as 7-day means and distance from each astronaut’s own baseline. Then 34 rules check them, and each rule cites a Value ID from the knowledge base. An Isolation Forest model flags unusual combinations that no single rule sees.
  4. Triage. One level per person per day, sent to the right role.
  5. Interface. Each alert shows its reason, the action to take, and a “Why?” panel with the NASA source and page.

A live replay sends one mission day per minute, and the engine reruns as each day arrives.
Live demo: https://orvitalis.us

Benefits

  • Each person sees only what they must act on, which reduces alert fatigue.
  • Every threshold traces to a NASA page, so medical staff can check an alert instead of trusting a black box.
  • Personal baselines catch changes that fixed limits miss.
  • In our tests, the engine caught 36 of 37 simulated risk scenarios and raised no false alarms on decoy data.

Intended impact
On long missions, crews will get less real-time help from Earth. ORVITALIS shows how onboard monitoring can spot risks early and send them to the right person while staying open to review. One example: crew short on sleep are flagged before a critical task such as a spacewalk.

Tools and technology

  • Software: Python, FastAPI, SQLite, pandas, NumPy and scikit-learn on the backend; React and Vite on the frontend.
  • Hosting: an Azure virtual machine with nginx and HTTPS. No special hardware.
  • NASA data: DONKI solar particle events, OSDR RadLab ISS radiation dose, OSDR RR-1 cabin CO₂, the HRP Evidence Reports and NASA-STD-3001.
  • AI use: we used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant for code and documentation. The team reviewed and tested all of it.

How it is creative
Most health dashboards show numbers. ORVITALIS shows where each number comes from. Every value is labelled as a NASA standard, a report finding, a study, or our own team design. Where NASA gives no limit, the system says so instead of guessing, and three rules stay switched off for that reason. Real ISS environment data from different missions is replayed on one simulated mission timeline, and each value keeps its original date and source.

Factors we considered

  • Data availability: we ran 33 queries on NASA OSDR (355 studies). No open dataset had human sleep, reaction time, mood, heart rate, blood pressure or SpO₂. So crew indicators are simulated from Evidence Report values, while radiation, CO₂ and space weather data are real.
  • Roles: escalation follows NASA’s medical structure.
  • Alert fatigue: one level per person per day.
  • Next steps: add a login per role, connect a real wearable and vehicle telemetry.
